title: LIS and tricky transitions
sub: Longest Increasing Subsequence from O(n²) to O(n log n) via tails and binary search, Regular Expression Matching and DP for “is it possible”
cards/0/title: LIS: the problem and an O(n²) solution
cards/0/body:
Longest Increasing Subsequence (LeetCode #300). Given an array of up to 2500 numbers, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence — the elements need not be adjacent, but they keep their original order. For [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18] the answer is 4: for example, 2, 3, 7, 18.

A subsequence, as in the previous lesson, signals DP over prefixes. State: dp[i] is the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at i. That makes it easy to extend: nums[i] can be appended to any subsequence that ends on a smaller number to its left.

Transition: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i], or 1 if there is none. Answer — the maximum over all dp[i], not dp[n − 1]: the longest one doesn’t have to end at the last element.

Cost: for every i we scan everything to its left — O(n²). For n = 2500 that is 3·10⁶ comparisons, which fits. But the problem asks right away: and in O(n log n)?
cards/1/task: Walk the dp filling for [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]. The rig will stop twice and ask which value the next number gets.
cards/1/goal/asks/0/q: dp = [1, 1, 1, 2] for 10, 9, 2, 5. The next number is 3. What goes into dp[4]?
cards/1/goal/asks/0/explain: Only a subsequence ending on a smaller number can be extended. To the left of 3 only 2 is smaller, and its dp = 1 — we get 2. The 5 with dp = 2 is larger than 3: 5, 3 isn’t increasing.
cards/1/goal/asks/1/q: dp[5] = 3 for 7, dp[6] = 4 for 101. The last number is 18. What goes into dp[7]?
cards/1/goal/asks/1/explain: Among the smaller ones to the left the best is 7 with dp = 3: 18 extends, for example, 2, 3, 7 — we get 4. 101 with dp = 4 is larger than 18 and doesn’t fit. The problem’s answer is the maximum over dp, also 4: two different subsequences of length 4 end on 101 and on 18.
cards/2/title: Tails: O(n log n) via binary search
cards/2/body:
What work does O(n²) repeat? For every number it searches all of the left part again for “the best thing to extend”. But for extending, what matters is not everything that came before, only one thing: which number a subsequence of a given length ends on. And of two subsequences of the same length, the one ending on the smaller number is better — more numbers can extend it.

Keep an array tails: tails[k] is the smallest last element among all increasing subsequences of length k + 1 found so far. Invariant: tails is strictly increasing (a subsequence of length k + 2 contains a subsequence of length k + 1 with a smaller end). So binary search works on it.

The step for a number x: find the first tails[k] ≥ x — that is lower_bound from the binary search unit. If there is none, x extends the longest one, append it. Otherwise set tails[k] = x: a subsequence of length k + 1 now ends on a smaller number. The length of tails at the end is the answer. Time O(n log n), memory O(n).

Important: tails itself is not an LIS. On [3, 4, 1] it becomes [1, 4], and there is no such subsequence: the 1 comes after the 4. Only the length matches.

Instead of your own lower_bound you can use List<int>.BinarySearch: in a strictly increasing list it finds an equal element, and if there is none it returns the ~index of the insertion point, like Array.BinarySearch.
cards/2/flow/3: the answer is the length of tails
cards/3/q: nums = [4, 10, 4, 3, 8, 9]. What will tails be after all steps, and what does the algorithm return?
cards/3/explain: 4 → [4]; 10 → [4, 10]; 4: the first ≥ 4 is tails[0], replace → [4, 10]; 3 → [3, 10]; 8: the first ≥ 8 is 10, replace → [3, 8]; 9 → [3, 8, 9]. Length 3 — and that is correct: for example, 4, 8, 9. Here tails [3, 8, 9] happens to be a subsequence too, but that isn’t always so — remember [3, 4, 1].
cards/3/wrong/1: The 3 replaces tails[0] = 4: the first element ≥ 3 is 4. A subsequence of length 1 now ends on a smaller number.
cards/3/wrong/2: That is the state after the third step. 3, 8 and 9 will still change the array: 8 replaces 10, and 9 is appended.
cards/3/wrong/3: The second 4 and the 3 don’t lengthen tails, they replace: no strictly increasing subsequence of length 4 can be built here.
cards/4/q: Build O(n log n) LIS on List<int>.BinarySearch.
cards/4/explain: A negative BinarySearch result is the ~index of the insertion point, and ~k gives it back; −k would be one index too far. An insertion point past the end means x is larger than every tail — append. Otherwise x becomes the new, smaller tail of length k + 1. If x is already in tails, BinarySearch returns its index — replacing with an equal value changes nothing, and strict increase is preserved. The answer is the length of tails, not n.
cards/5/q: This LIS returns 3 instead of 1 on [2, 2, 2]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: With <= the search finds the first tails[k] > x — that is upper_bound, and an equal number is appended at the end: [2] → [2, 2] → [2, 2, 2]. That computes the longest non-decreasing subsequence. A strictly increasing one needs lower_bound — the first tails[k] ≥ x, that is the condition tails[mid] < x.
cards/6/title: Regular Expression Matching: “is it possible” is DP too
cards/6/body:
Regular Expression Matching (LeetCode #10). A string s and a pattern p, up to 20 characters each. The pattern has letters, . — any single character, and * — zero or more copies of the preceding element. The whole string must match. “aab” and “c*a*b” — yes: c* takes zero c’s, a* — two a’s.

The answer is yes/no, there is nothing to minimize. But at every x* there is a choice: how many characters it eats. And what follows depends only on the position — how many characters of the string and the pattern have been consumed. A choice plus a subproblem by position is DP, where a cell holds a bool and the transition is an “or” over the options.

State: dp[i, j] — does s[..i] match p[..j]. Base: dp[0, 0] = true; the empty string matches a prefix like “a*b*”, so dp[0, j] = p[j − 1] == '*' && dp[0, j − 2].

Transition. If p[j − 1] is a letter or a dot, it must match s[i − 1], and the rest is the diagonal dp[i − 1, j − 1]. If p[j − 1] == '*', the pair x* has two options: zero copies — drop the pair, dp[i, j − 2]; one more copy — x matches s[i − 1], and that character is eaten by the same pair: dp[i − 1, j].

Time and memory O(m·n) — 441 cells for 20 × 20.
cards/7/task: Walk the table for s = “aab”, p = “c*a*b”: rows are prefixes of the string, columns are prefixes of the pattern, ✓ — matches, · — doesn’t. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes into a cell.
cards/7/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: ·: the characters matched, but the diagonal is ·
cards/7/goal/asks/0/q: Cell (2, 3): “aa” versus “c*a”. The last characters are “a” and “a”. The diagonal dp[1, 2] — “a” versus “c*” — is ·. What goes in?
cards/7/goal/asks/0/explain: A pattern letter eats exactly one character of the string, and the diagonal checks the rest: “a” versus “c*” doesn’t match, so neither does “aa” versus “c*a”. A single letter “a” in the pattern can’t cover two. Only the “*” transition looks at the cell above.
cards/7/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: ✓: “a*” eats one more “a” — take the cell above
cards/7/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: ·: “*” isn’t a character, there is nothing to compare
cards/7/goal/asks/1/q: Cell (2, 4): “aa” versus “c*a*”. Zero copies — dp[2, 2] = ·, above dp[1, 4] = ✓. What goes in?
cards/7/goal/asks/1/explain: For “*” the two options are joined by “or”. Zero copies didn’t fit, but “one more copy” does: the “a” before the “*” equals s[1], and the cell above dp[1, 4] says “a” is already covered by the pattern “c*a*”. The same pair a* eats the second “a” too: ✓.
cards/8/q: Why does the “one more copy” option for “*” look at dp[i − 1, j] and not at dp[i − 1, j − 2]?
cards/8/options/0: dp[i − 1, j] keeps the pair x* in the pattern, so it can eat more characters; dp[i − 1, j − 2] would allow it exactly one copy
cards/8/options/1: dp[i − 1, j − 2] goes outside the table when j = 2
cards/8/options/2: There is no difference: both options produce the same tables
cards/8/options/3: dp[i − 1, j] is the “zero copies” option, and dp[i − 1, j − 2] is “one copy”
cards/8/explain: Cell (i − 1, j) has the same pair x* at the end of the pattern and a string one character shorter. If it is ✓, x* has already covered some characters, and s[i − 1] is one more. That way one formula allows any number of copies. With (i − 1, j − 2) the pair would eat exactly s[i − 1] and nothing else: “aaa” versus “a*” would become ·.
cards/8/wrong/1: With j = 2 the index j − 2 = 0 is the legitimate column of the empty pattern. It is not about bounds but about the number of copies.
cards/8/wrong/2: There is a difference: on “aaa” and “a*” the j − 2 option gives ·, although a* covers three a’s.
cards/8/wrong/3: Zero copies is dp[i, j − 2]: the string doesn’t get shorter, the pair is dropped. dp[i − 1, j] shortens the string — that is a copy.
cards/9/title: How to recognize DP, and where else these transitions appear
cards/9/body:
“I see DP” — when three signs come together: the question asks for a count, a minimum/maximum or whether it is possible; every step has a choice; what follows depends on a small state (a position, a sum, a pair of indices), not on the whole history. Then out loud: “the state is …, the transition goes over the choice of …, there are so many cells, so much work per cell — in total …”.

Word Break (#139): can a string be cut into dictionary words? dp[i] — can the prefix of length i be split; dp[i] = true if there is j < i with dp[j] and the word s[j..i) in the dictionary.

Wildcard Matching (#44): ? is any character, * is any sequence. The star stands alone: dp[i, j − 1] || dp[i − 1, j] — empty, or it eats one more character.

LIS in problems: Russian Doll Envelopes (#354) — sort by width, and for equal widths by height descending, then LIS over the heights. A non-decreasing subsequence — upper_bound instead of lower_bound. n − LIS is the minimum number of elements to move (take out and reinsert elsewhere) to sort a list.

In a game: filters with * in a console or an asset search (“enemy_*”, “*_lod0”) are Wildcard Matching. When a list of UI elements is updated, an LIS over the new positions shows which elements can stay put — only the rest move (some UI frameworks minimize node moves exactly this way).
cards/9/deep:
Recovering an LIS in O(n log n). Store indices in tails instead of values, plus a parent array: when nums[i] lands at position k, its parent is the index that was in tails[k − 1]. At the end walk from tails[len − 1] along parent — you get the subsequence backwards. The number of distinct LIS (#673) can’t be counted this way — that needs the O(n²) version with a “length, count” pair, or a segment tree.

Why tails is correct. The invariant “tails[k] is the minimal end of length k + 1” is preserved: x extends a subsequence of length k (its end tails[k − 1] < x) and gives length k + 1 ending in x ≤ tails[k]; positions right of k are untouched: x can’t extend a subsequence of length k + 1, since its smallest end tails[k] ≥ x. This is related to dealing cards into piles (patience sorting): the number of piles equals the LIS length.

Regex top-down. A recursion Match(i, j) over the same transitions, memoized by (i, j), is also O(m·n) and often easier to explain. Without memory it is exponential in the worst case: the pattern “a*a*a*a*b” on a string of only a’s tries every way of distributing the characters among the stars, and each extra star multiplies their number by roughly the string length.

.NET Regex. The System.Text.RegularExpressions engine backtracks by default — like our recursion without memory — and on patterns like (a+)+$ time grows exponentially (catastrophic backtracking, the basis of ReDoS attacks). Protection: a timeout in the Regex constructor (the matchTimeout parameter, available since .NET Framework 4.5) and, since .NET 7, RegexOptions.NonBacktracking — linear time in the input length, without backreferences and lookarounds. Unity doesn’t have this mode (it arrived in .NET 7), so user input goes into Regex only with a timeout, or into your own simple matcher like the Wildcard DP. RegexOptions.Compiled does nothing in Unity: Unity’s class library comes from Mono, which ignores this flag — both on Mono and under IL2CPP, where generating IL at runtime isn’t possible anyway.
cards/10/options/0: In Word Break dp[i] means the prefix of length i can be split into words
cards/10/options/1: In Wildcard Matching “*” gives the transition dp[i, j − 1] || dp[i − 1, j]
cards/10/options/2: After the pass, tails is one of the longest increasing subsequences
cards/10/options/3: A non-decreasing subsequence needs upper_bound in tails
cards/10/options/4: If the answer is yes/no, DP isn’t needed: there is nothing to minimize
cards/10/explain: Word Break is DP over prefixes with a bool in each cell. The Wildcard star is empty (the column to the left) or eats a character (the row above). tails holds the best ends for every length, but may not itself be a subsequence: [3, 4, 1] → [1, 4]. For non-decreasing, equal numbers must extend — upper_bound. “Is it possible” is as much a reason for DP as a minimum: a bool cell, an “or” transition.
cards/11/q: You are solving Regular Expression Matching out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: must the whole string match or a part? what can precede “*”? lengths?
cards/11/items/1: Naive recursion: at every x*, try every number of copies — exponential
cards/11/items/2: The state dp[i, j] — does s[..i] match p[..j]; the base dp[0, 0] and the row for “x*”
cards/11/items/3: Transitions: letter or dot — diagonal; “*” — zero copies dp[i, j − 2] or one more dp[i − 1, j]
cards/11/items/4: Run “aa” and “a*”: ✓ via “one more copy” twice
cards/11/items/6: Edge cases: the empty string versus “a*b*”, the pattern “.*”
cards/11/explain: Clarifying “the whole string” changes the answer for “aab” and “a”. The recursion explains where the transitions come from, the table how to get rid of the exponent. Running “aa” against “a*” checks the subtlest transition right away.
cards/12/q: Match the problem with its state or technique.
cards/12/pairs/0/1: dp[i] — the longest one ending at i
cards/12/pairs/2/1: dp[i, j]: zero copies or one more
cards/12/pairs/3/1: dp[i] — the prefix splits into words
